newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa apartheid police point out burial sites.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa apartheid police point out burial sites.

text.p: Six former South African policemen seeking amnesty for past crimes have pointed out burial sites where bodies of anti-apartheid activists were dumped, an investigating commission said on Wednesday.

The security policemen are requesting amnesty from prosecution for the murders of 10 people from Nobel laureate Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which is probing crimes committed by both sides of the apartheid divide.

"(Six) former security policemen...have led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's investigators to five sites throughout KwaZulu-Natal where they murdered and then disposed of the bodies of 10 former political activists," commission spokesman Mdu Lembede said in a statement.

He said commission investigators working with pathologists and other experts had uncovered two bodies on a farm on the north coast of the Indian Ocean province, and were working to exhume another two bodies.
"This was not the only farm that the security police used in the area. We think that there is far more to this than meets the eye," Lembede told Reuters.

"They ran these farms in the same style as Vlakplaas," he said, referring to a now-disbanded covert police unit based near Pretoria which murdered and tortured opponents of the minority white government.
A former Vlakplaas commander, Eugene de Kock, is currently serving two life sentences and an additional 212 years in jail for a series of murders and lesser crimes.

The six ex-policemen now seeking amnesty in KwaZulu-Natal -- the volatile Zulu heartland of South Africa -- have confessed to throwing two bodies into a river after shooting their victims, Lembede said.
"The applicants also confirmed that four more people were blown up in such a way that very little remained of their bodies," he said.
The names of the policemen and their victims are known to the commission but Lembede said the names of the victims would not be released until their families had been notified.
The commission, which has until the end of this year to look into 30 years of human rights abuses, has the power to grant perpetrators amnesty if they confess in full to their crimes.
